subject: Computer Networking
title: Why Redundancy Matters
description: Learn Why Redundancy Matters in one minute.

hook.text: Every major outage shares one trait: a single point of failure that nobody planned around.

buildup.text: Redundancy means backups at every layer: multiple cables, data centers, DNS providers, and power feeds.

discovery.text: N+1 adds one extra of everything. N+2 adds two. The more critical the system, the more spares it needs.

twist.text: Redundancy costs money. Many skip it until an outage proves downtime costs far more.

climax.text: Netflix built Chaos Monkey — it randomly kills production servers to ensure redundancy actually works.

punchline.text: If you haven't tested your backup, you don't have one.

quiz.question: What does Netflix's Chaos Monkey do?
options: Randomly kills production servers to test redundancy

details.summary: Network redundancy means having multiple independent paths for data so that the failure of any single component does not cause an outage. Every major outage teaches the same lesson: systems that seemed redundant had hidden single points of failure.
details.whyItMatters: Redundancy is the fundamental principle of reliable networking. Understanding where your real single points of failure hide is the difference between planned resilience and unexpected disaster.
takeaways: Redundancy requires truly independent failure domains
Hidden shared dependencies defeat apparent redundancy
Regular failure testing reveals gaps in redundancy design

faq.question: What is the most common mistake in redundancy design?
faq.answer: Assuming systems are independent when they share a hidden dependency. Two servers in the same rack share power. Two network paths through the same building share a fiber entrance. True redundancy requires mapping all shared dependencies and eliminating each one.

faq.question: How do companies test whether their redundancy works?
faq.answer: Chaos engineering practices like Netflix's Chaos Monkey deliberately kill components in production to verify that redundancy works. Game day exercises simulate major failures. Companies that do not regularly test their failover often discover it is broken during real incidents.
